analysis.one_liner: Creates an independent federal board to investigate police custody deaths, officer-involved shootings, and severe uses of force.
analysis.headline: Introduced on December 8, 2020 with 8 Democratic sponsors, the bill was referred to committee and died there 26 days later when the Congress ended, without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new independent federal agency, the National Police Misuse of Force Investigation Board, with eight Senate-confirmed members split between the parties. It would investigate every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe injury, with subpoena power, access to weapons and autopsies, and public reports. States and cities that take certain federal justice grants would have to let the board's findings be used in criminal and civil court cases and file yearly reports on reforms, or lose up to 10 percent of those grant funds. The bill would also give victims' families a federal point of contact and taxpayer-funded counseling.
analysis.who_benefits: Families of people killed or seriously injured by police, and communities seeking independent accounts of these incidents. Families would get a designated federal contact, help arranging counseling through an experienced nonprofit, advance briefings before public announcements, and invitations to hearings [S3]. The public would get a searchable record of each incident with demographic data on victims and officers, plus annual statistics to Congress [S3]. Prosecutors and civil plaintiffs in grant-receiving states could present board findings to juries [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of people killed by police

how_it_helps.text: Establishes an independent board that must investigate and report the facts and probable cause of every death in police custody, officer-involved shooting, and use of force causing severe bodily injury [S3].
Grants the board subpoena power, entry to incident scenes, control over testing of involved weapons, and authority to order autopsies [S3].
Makes board records publicly available on request, with incident reports including victim and officer demographics, the reason for the stop, and the outcome [S3].

Requires family support services: a named federal point of contact, a designated nonprofit providing mental health and counseling, and guarantees that families are briefed before public announcements and can attend hearings [S3].

Ties certain DOJ law enforcement grants to compliance: states and localities must make board findings admissible in criminal and civil court, present them to juries, and file yearly progress reports, or face a reduction of 1 to 10 percent of funds under the Byrne and JAG programs [S2] [S3].
Lets the DOJ Civil Rights Division open pattern-or-practice investigations citing a grant recipient's failure to act on board recommendations as evidence of a systemic problem [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State and local police departments and governments, which face federal investigations, court-admissible findings, yearly reporting, and possible grant cuts; police officers, whose cases could include board findings presented to a jury; and taxpayers, who fund the new agency's staff, offices, and at least one investigator in every state far from a regional office [S3].

drawbacks.text: The board's recommendations are advisory: a recipient can formally refuse a recommendation so long as it gives written reasons and a timetable, and enforcement runs only through grant reductions and discretionary DOJ pattern-or-practice cases [S3].

Board reports cannot be admitted or used in civil damage lawsuits arising from the incident, which limits one path families might otherwise use the findings for, even as the grant condition makes findings admissible in court cases generally [S3].

The bill text contains language copied from aviation-accident law, including a conflict-of-interest rule for members with a stake in an 'aviation enterprise,' duties to evaluate the 'transportation safety consciousness' of agencies, and evaluations of hazardous-materials transport safeguards, indicating it was not fully adapted to policing [S3].

Opponents of federal leverage over local policing would object that conditioning DOJ grants and overriding state court rules on evidence presses states to conform their laws to a federal board's findings [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give families and the public something that mostly does not exist today: an independent national account of police deaths and shootings, plus real support services for survivors. Its enforcement teeth are limited — recommendations can be refused in writing, and the only automatic penalty is a modest 1 to 10 percent cut to certain grants. The drafting is sloppy, with leftover aviation language, and the bar on using board reports in civil suits undercuts one of the main ways families seek accountability. On balance it is a genuine accountability measure with real limits, and it never got far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last month of the two-year Congress, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and a Transportation subcommittee and stayed there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on December 8, 2020, in the final weeks of the 116th Congress [S1] [S5].
Seven Democratic colleagues cosponsored it; no Republicans did [S4].

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and then on December 9 to the Transportation Subcommittee on Economic Development, Public Buildings, and Emergency Management [S5].
No further action was taken before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, so the bill expired without a hearing or vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments and officers avoided a federal investigative board whose findings could be presented to juries and whose recommendations could cost states and cities up to 10 percent of certain DOJ grants. No one gained the accountability the bill offered.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Police Misuse of Force Investigation Board Act on December 8, 2020.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; all eight sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but the record does not show active opposition either.

industries.industry: State and local police departments and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The board would investigate custody deaths, shootings, and severe-force incidents, and its findings could be presented to juries in cases against officers; departments that receive covered DOJ grants must act on recommendations or lose 1 to 10 percent of those funds. Departments' ability to control their own incident investigations and records would be substantially curtailed.

Federal investigators with subpoena power and autopsy authority would examine incidents involving officers, and board findings would be admissible in criminal and civil proceedings in grant-receiving states. Officers also gain one protection: board reports themselves could not be used in civil damage suits.

The board must designate an experienced nonprofit to coordinate counseling and emotional support for victims and families of each incident, creating a federally funded service role. Their interest runs alongside families'.
